questions.q: What does an SCD Type 2 change do when a tracked attribute changes?
options: Closes out the existing row (setting its expiration date and current flag) and inserts a brand-new row with a new surrogate key for the new version
Overwrites the existing row in place, keeping no history
Adds a new column to the same row to hold the previous value
Deletes the old row entirely and replaces it with a new one that reuses the same surrogate key
questions.explain: Type 2 preserves history by keeping the old row intact (marked no longer current) and inserting a new, separately-keyed row for the current version — that's the defining update-then-insert mechanic.

questions.q: In the real Microsoft diagram used in this lesson, why does the new version of the salesperson row get a brand-new surrogate key (369) instead of reusing the old one (296)?
options: Because the natural key (EmployeeID) is now duplicated across two rows, and the surrogate key is what makes each version uniquely addressable for fact table joins
Because surrogate keys must always increase by exactly one digit
Because SQL Server automatically deletes the old surrogate key when a row is updated
Surrogate keys are irrelevant to Type 2 — only the natural key matters
questions.explain: With two rows now sharing the same natural key, only a unique surrogate key per version lets fact tables join to the exact version that was current when each fact occurred.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the IsCurrentFlag (or IsCurrent) column in a Type 2 dimension?
options: It marks exactly one version per natural key as the current one that new fact loads should use
It stores the total count of all historical versions for that member
It determines whether the row is a fact row or a dimension row
It has no functional purpose — it's purely cosmetic
questions.explain: IsCurrentFlag lets ETL processes and queries quickly filter to the single active version of each dimension member without having to compare validity date ranges.

questions.q: What real tradeoff does Type 2 introduce, according to this lesson?
options: The fact table's effective grain becomes "dimension member version" rather than just "dimension member," and rapidly changing attributes can produce an overwhelming number of versions
Type 2 makes all historical rollups permanently inaccurate
Type 2 requires deleting all existing fact table rows before it can be implemented
There is no tradeoff — Type 2 has no downsides compared to Type 1
questions.explain: Type 2 gets correct historical rollups, but at the cost of more rows to manage per dimension member — and an attribute that changes very frequently can generate an unmanageable number of versions, which is a signal to reconsider the design.

questions.q: Why does this lesson connect Type 2 back to Lesson 12's insistence that dimensions use surrogate keys rather than natural keys alone?
options: Because Type 2 versioning is very difficult to retrofit cleanly onto a dimension that was only ever keyed by its natural key
Because natural keys are always numeric and surrogate keys are always text
Because Type 2 doesn't actually need any kind of key at all
Because surrogate keys were only introduced for performance reasons unrelated to history tracking
questions.explain: Once a natural key repeats across multiple stored versions, only a separate surrogate key can uniquely identify each version — which is exactly why surrogate keys are treated as non-negotiable earlier in this course.
